paragraphs: CHEMREASONER approaches catalyst discovery as an iterative computational search. A language model proposes chemical hypotheses, while feedback from atomistic graph neural networks helps assess the resulting candidates. This connects reasoning expressed in language with evaluations grounded in three-dimensional atomic structures, giving the search a way to revise its direction as evidence accumulates.

Candidates encountered during the search undergo structural evaluation that considers spatial orientation, reaction pathways, and stability. Scores based on adsorption energies and reaction energy barriers then guide further exploration. These quantities connect candidate selection to the energetics of the chemical process, so the language model’s suggestions are assessed using more than their linguistic plausibility.

The paper also introduces planning methods that guide exploration automatically, without human input during that exploration. The authors report competitive performance against implementations built around chemical descriptors enumerated by experts. The contribution is a computational screening framework that combines proposal generation, structural evaluation, and energy-based feedback to search for promising catalysts.
icml-2024-chemreasoner-heuristic-search-.tldr: CHEMREASONER combines language-model hypotheses with atomistic chemical feedback to automatically search for promising catalysts.

paragraphs: Bayesian neural networks use sampling to represent uncertainty over possible networks, but their large and structured parameter spaces make this difficult. This paper examines that difficulty through the relationship between a network’s weights and the function those weights produce. Its central perspective is that understanding sampling requires considering both the parameter description and the resulting predictive behavior.

The authors identify a systematic connection between overparameterization and the difficulty of sampling. This makes network size and structure relevant to how an inference procedure should be organized and assessed. Through extensive experiments, they develop practical guidance for sampling and for diagnosing convergence, addressing both how to obtain samples and how to judge whether the sampling process is behaving adequately.

The resulting approach initializes sampling using a deep ensemble. The authors present it as an effective method with competitive predictive performance and uncertainty quantification. The stated result supports the feasibility of sample-based inference when its design accounts for the weight–function relationship; it does not establish mode-connectedness as a universally necessary condition.
icml-2024-connecting-the-dots-is-mode-co.tldr: The paper connects Bayesian neural-network sampling difficulty to overparameterization and develops an effective approach initialized with a deep ensemble.

paragraphs: A feature can be useful in one context and uninformative in another. Selecting one shared feature set for an entire population can overlook this variation. The paper addresses the additional subtlety that context may change which features matter even when the context variable does not directly affect the outcome being predicted.

Conditional Stochastic Gates, or c-STG, selects features using gates whose probabilities depend on context. Each gate is modeled with a conditional Bernoulli variable, representing a probabilistic decision to include a feature. A hypernetwork maps context variables to the parameters controlling these gates. The gates and the prediction model are learned together, allowing feature selection to adapt to the circumstances of a prediction.

The theoretical analysis indicates that this architecture can offer greater flexibility and better performance than population-level selection in complex settings. Benchmarks on simulated and real datasets across multiple domains also show potential improvements in selection, prediction accuracy, and interpretability. The explanation becomes contextual: it concerns which inputs matter under particular conditions, rather than only which inputs matter overall.
icml-2024-contextual-feature-selection-w.tldr: c-STG learns context-dependent feature-selection probabilities, enabling more flexible prediction and interpretation than a single shared feature set.

paragraphs: EnzyGen designs enzymes by jointly generating an amino acid sequence and its three-dimensional coordinates. Generation is guided by sites important for function and by the substrate associated with the desired catalytic activity. The sites are mined automatically from enzyme databases, connecting the design process to functional information already available about enzymes.

The model alternates attention layers with neighborhood equivariant layers. This architecture captures relationships across the full protein sequence alongside local influences among amino acids that are close in three-dimensional space. Training combines objectives for sequence generation, position prediction, and enzyme–substrate interaction, so the model learns these connected aspects of design together.

The authors also introduce EnzyBench, containing 3,157 enzyme families and covering the enzymes available in the Protein Data Bank. They report the best performance across all 323 testing families and a 10.79% improvement over the strongest baseline in substrate binding affinity. These results support the approach’s ability to produce well-folded designs with favorable binding to specified substrates, while the stated numerical comparison concerns binding affinity.
icml-2024-generative-enzyme-design-guide.tldr: EnzyGen jointly generates enzyme sequences and structures from functional sites and substrates, reporting improved substrate binding across its testing families.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning that combines an existing dataset with new interaction in an environment. The offline dataset contains only states, without the actions or rewards usually assumed available. The goal is to compete with the best policy covered by that data while using online experience to support learning.

The authors distinguish two forms of access to the environment. A reset model can restart from any state, while a trace model can restart only from initial states and must generate full trajectories. They provide evidence that competing with the covered policy is hard under trace access without an additional condition on the offline data.

That condition, admissibility, requires that the offline data could have been produced by the policy class under consideration. Under these assumptions, the proposed algorithm provably matches the performance of algorithms using the stronger reset model. Proof-of-concept experiments suggest practical effectiveness. The key contribution is therefore conditional: observation-only data can support strong hybrid learning under trace access when it is compatible with the policy class.
icml-2024-hybrid-reinforcement-learning-.tldr: Under admissibility assumptions, observation-only offline data enables a trace-access RL algorithm to match the performance of algorithms with stronger reset access.

paragraphs: The paper studies large nonconvex optimization problems whose variables must remain nonnegative. These include nonnegative least squares, matrix factorization, and some problems involving sparsity-inducing regularization. Simple gradient methods can progress slowly on ill-conditioned problems or linger near saddle regions, while methods using curvature often require difficult internal optimization steps.

The starting point is a two-metric projection framework. Near the boundary of the feasible region, it uses projected gradient steps; in the interior, it uses Newton steps. This division allows the method to use curvature information while preserving nonnegativity through a simple projection. The authors extend the framework by solving its subproblems approximately and incorporating directions of non-positive curvature.

These changes make the framework suitable for large-scale, nonconvex settings, where exact subproblem solutions can be demanding and saddle behavior matters. The authors establish state-of-the-art convergence rates for several classes of nonconvex problems and report competitive practical results across a variety of problems. The theoretical claims concern those problem classes, while the experiments demonstrate how the methods perform in practice.
icml-2024-inexact-newton-type-methods-fo.tldr: The paper extends projected Newton methods with approximate subproblem solutions and non-positive curvature directions for large nonconvex problems with nonnegative variables.

paragraphs: This paper develops a tool that extracts logic-tree explanations for observed event sequences using a language model. A temporal point process supplies a likelihood score, allowing proposed explanations to be evaluated against the events. The language model supplies prior knowledge about plausible rules, while the observations influence which explanations receive support.

The method treats the logic tree as a hidden variable within an amortized Expectation-Maximization framework. In the E-step, it combines the language-model prior with event likelihoods to form a posterior over trees. Because this discrete combinatorial space does not yield a closed-form solution, a learnable GFlowNet generates diverse samples intended to represent that posterior.

In the M-step, the sampled rules approximate averaging over possible explanations and support updates to model parameters and tunable prior parameters. For online use, a lightweight local model iteratively extracts relevant rules for each sequence in only a few iterations. Empirical demonstrations show promising performance and adaptability, supporting the combination of language-based rule proposals with statistical evaluation of observed events.
icml-2024-latent-logic-tree-extraction-f.tldr: The method combines language-model priors, event likelihoods, and GFlowNet sampling to learn logic-tree explanations tailored to event sequences.

paragraphs: Emergency services can reposition idle responders to cover gaps left by dispatches or changing demand. Choosing an allocation is difficult because the number of possible assignments grows rapidly and future requests are uncertain. The paper targets the decision time of an existing hierarchical approach that divides the problem spatially and performs online Monte Carlo tree search.

The proposed method retains the hierarchical decomposition but replaces online search with reinforcement learning. Actor-critic agents use transformers to accommodate states and actions whose dimensions vary. Additional projections turn complex states into fixed-dimensional observations, and combinatorial techniques translate continuous actions into discrete responder allocations. Together, these components address the mismatch between the allocation problem and the representations used by the learning system.

Experiments using real-world data from Nashville and Seattle report a three-orders-of-magnitude reduction in computation time per decision relative to the state of the art. Average ambulance response time also decreases slightly, by five seconds. In these evaluations, faster computation therefore accompanies a modest improvement in the operational outcome the repositioning decisions are intended to support.
icml-2024-multi-agent-reinforcement-lear.tldr: Hierarchical reinforcement learning cuts responder-repositioning decision time by three orders of magnitude while reducing average ambulance response time by five seconds in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Combining tissue-slide images with gene-expression profiles can support cancer survival prediction, but the inputs create a substantial computational burden. A slide may contribute more than ten thousand patch tokens, alongside tokens representing gene groups. Processing all of them with attention requires considerable memory and makes later interpretation more complicated.

The paper proposes summarizing these inputs through prototypes learned without supervision. Morphological prototypes condense the visual content of a slide, while biological pathway prototypes encode the transcriptomic profile in terms of cellular functions. The proposed image summary targets more than 300-fold compression. A fusion network then combines a small, fixed set of multimodal tokens using either a Transformer or optimal transport cross-alignment, without approximations at that fusion stage.

Evaluation across six cancer types shows better performance than state-of-the-art methods with substantially less computation. The compact representation also enables new interpretability analyses. The approach matters because its summaries address both the cost of combining large biological inputs and the difficulty of examining how those inputs contribute to survival predictions.
icml-2024-multimodal-prototyping-for-can.tldr: Unsupervised morphological and pathway prototypes compactly combine tissue images and gene expression, improving survival prediction and computational efficiency across six cancer types.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether offline actor-critic reinforcement learning can scale to large models, including transformers. It studies multi-task learning from a large dataset spanning 132 continuous-control tasks, with both expert and suboptimal behavior. This setting tests whether learning from stored experience can support a broad policy when the demonstrations vary in quality.

The authors introduce a Perceiver-based actor-critic architecture and identify features needed to make offline reinforcement learning work with self-attention and cross-attention. Their results show scaling behavior similar to supervised learning. They also find that offline actor-critic algorithms can outperform strong behavioral-cloning baselines, which learn by imitating the behaviors recorded in the dataset.

The findings support simple offline actor-critic methods as a practical route beyond relying primarily on behavioral cloning. The authors report that offline reinforcement learning can produce multi-task policies that handle many domains simultaneously, including real robotics tasks, using suboptimal demonstrations or self-generated data. The significance is the demonstrated compatibility of large attention-based models, diverse tasks, and data that need not consist entirely of expert behavior.
icml-2024-offline-actor-critic-reinforce.tldr: Offline actor-critic reinforcement learning scales to large attention-based models and can outperform strong behavioral-cloning baselines across diverse control tasks.

paragraphs: Constrained optimization provides a way to specify behaviors that a neural network should satisfy. A common formulation introduces Lagrange multipliers and turns training into a min-max problem. Updating the model and multipliers through gradient descent-ascent can produce unstable oscillations, making reliable multiplier updates an important obstacle to using constraints in practice.

The paper proposes νPI, an update algorithm based on proportional-integral controllers, and analyzes it from an optimization perspective. It provides theoretical and empirical explanations for why momentum methods fail to resolve the shortcomings of gradient descent-ascent. This analysis is paired with empirical evidence that the proposed controller handles multiplier dynamics successfully.

The authors also prove that νPI generalizes popular momentum methods in single-objective minimization, connecting the controller approach to familiar optimization tools. In experiments, νPI reliably stabilizes multiplier updates, and its hyperparameters behave robustly and predictably. These results support a more manageable approach to constrained training, while the stabilization evidence reported here is experimental rather than an unrestricted guarantee for every constrained problem.
icml-2024-on-pi-controllers-for-updating.tldr: νPI uses proportional-integral control for Lagrange multiplier updates, empirically stabilizing constrained optimization while generalizing familiar momentum methods.

paragraphs: A single-camera video can be consistent with infinitely many underlying dynamic three-dimensional scenes. Methods that seek one plausible reconstruction typically add depth or geometry constraints to select a solution. OSN instead aims to represent the range of plausible scene configurations that agree with the observed video.

The central mechanism combines an object scale network with joint optimization to learn a scale range for each moving three-dimensional object. These ranges allow the framework to sample many configurations consistent with the input. Treating scale as a range makes ambiguity part of the representation, rather than forcing the method to commit immediately to a single configuration.

Experiments on multiple synthetic and real-world datasets report better dynamic novel-view synthesis accuracy than all evaluated baselines. The authors particularly emphasize improved recovery of fine-grained scene geometry. These findings support the usefulness of representing alternative configurations for reconstruction and rendering. Learning all plausible scenes is the framework’s stated goal; the reported mechanism enables sampling many faithful configurations rather than establishing exhaustive recovery of every possibility.
icml-2024-osn-infinite-representations-o.tldr: OSN learns object-scale ranges to sample multiple plausible dynamic 3D scenes from one video, improving novel-view synthesis and fine geometry in evaluations.

paragraphs: This position paper asks how AI systems can serve people with diverse values and perspectives. It develops a roadmap for pluralistic alignment using language models as a test bed. The central contribution is to separate several meanings of pluralism so that researchers can specify which behavior they want a model to exhibit.

Overton pluralism means presenting a spectrum of reasonable responses. Steerable pluralism means being able to adopt particular perspectives. Distributional pluralism means matching a specified population’s distribution of perspectives in a calibrated way. The paper also formalizes benchmark categories that assess multiple objectives, responsiveness to different trade-offs, and diverse human judgments through a jury-style evaluation.

Using this framework, the authors argue that current alignment techniques may face fundamental limits in supporting pluralism. Evidence from their experiments and prior work suggests that standard alignment procedures might reduce distributional pluralism. The roadmap therefore makes evaluation more precise: success at presenting several views or following a requested perspective does not by itself establish that a model reflects a population’s diversity.
icml-2024-position-a-roadmap-to-pluralis.tldr: The paper defines three forms of pluralistic alignment and corresponding benchmark approaches, arguing that standard alignment may reduce representation of diverse perspectives.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that black-box optimization and experimental design offer substantial opportunities for foundation models. It frames the field around sequence-based models and connects that perspective to existing research. The contribution is a research agenda for integrating language and sequence modeling into optimization, rather than a reported benchmark victory for one new algorithm.

One proposed direction uses information contained in free-form text to improve understanding of an optimization task. A second uses flexible sequence architectures, such as Transformers, to develop better optimization strategies. These directions concern different parts of the process: interpreting what a task involves and deciding how to search for good solutions.

A third direction concerns predicting performance in search spaces that have not previously been encountered. Together, the proposals suggest using foundation models both to incorporate broader task knowledge and to support optimization across unfamiliar settings. The authors present these as promising ways to reshape the field, organizing future work around capabilities that language and sequence models may bring to experimental design.
icml-2024-position-leverage-foundational.tldr: This position paper proposes using foundation models for task understanding, optimization strategy design, and performance prediction in unfamiliar search spaces.

paragraphs: Magnetic confinement fusion could eventually provide reliable carbon-free energy, but technical obstacles remain. This position paper identifies research problems where the authors believe machine learning can make useful contributions. Its purpose is to help ML researchers connect their methods to concrete priorities in fusion energy.

The agenda covers six areas: predicting disruptions, modeling simulations and dynamics, resolving partially observed data, improving control, choosing experiments through optimal design, and discovering materials. For each area, the paper supplies background, reviews previous machine-learning efforts, suggests desirable properties of future models, and discusses development challenges specific to the application.

The authors also consider efforts to improve the fusion data ecosystem and opportunities that may become accessible as both the technology and its data infrastructure mature. This makes data development part of the research agenda alongside modeling. The paper’s claim is prospective: fusion offers promising ways for machine-learning practitioners to contribute to decarbonization, while realizing those opportunities depends on progress in the technical problems and supporting infrastructure it describes.
icml-2024-position-opportunities-exist-f.tldr: The paper identifies six fusion-energy research priorities where machine learning could contribute, alongside the data infrastructure needed to support progress.

paragraphs: The paper models interpersonal coordination as a hidden process that helps explain statistical influence between people over time. One person’s state may influence another person’s later state, as reflected in observed behavior. The proposed definition measures coordination through how strongly state distributions are merged at the next relevant time point.

The authors first test the model on synthetic data. These experiments check whether the formal definition behaves as expected and whether generated coordination can be recovered despite noise. They then infer coordination from speech vocal characteristics and semantic content for 36 three-person teams completing two successive virtual search-and-rescue missions.

Across two datasets, inferred coordination generally predicts team scores on the second mission, but not on the first, when participants are largely learning the game. Adding semantic information improves prediction in some scenarios. The findings therefore connect the model’s coordination estimates with useful aspects of team performance, while showing that the relationship depends on mission stage and that the added modality is not uniformly beneficial.
icml-2024-probabilistic-modeling-of-inte.tldr: A probabilistic coordination model inferred from team speech generally predicts performance on a second search-and-rescue mission, but not the initial learning mission.

paragraphs: RichCLD studies reinforcement learning in environments where an agent observes high-dimensional inputs but the underlying state is low-dimensional. The framework assumes continuous latent dynamics with Lipschitz regularity, a condition controlling how sharply the dynamics can change. This setting separates the complexity of what the agent sees from the smaller state governing the environment.

The authors introduce an algorithm that is provably efficient in both statistical and computational terms within this framework. Its core is a new representation-learning objective. They show that objectives designed for discrete dynamics do not transfer naturally to continuous dynamics, making the representation objective a substantive part of the solution.

The objective is suitable for practical implementation and compares favorably with previous schemes under a standard evaluation protocol. The paper also establishes limits on which smoothness assumptions suffice: certain notions of Lipschitzness that permit sample-efficient learning without rich observations are insufficient when observations are rich. The guarantees consequently depend on the framework’s structure, rather than following from continuity or smoothness alone.
icml-2024-rich-observation-reinforcement.tldr: RichCLD provides an efficient RL algorithm for rich observations with continuous low-dimensional latent dynamics, while clarifying which regularity assumptions are insufficient.

paragraphs: Multi-agent debate asks language-model agents to exchange reasoning in pursuit of more accurate answers. This paper benchmarks debate and prompting strategies while considering cost, time, and accuracy. The comparison tests whether the extra interaction provides dependable benefits over approaches such as self-consistency and ensembles of multiple reasoning paths.

The authors find that existing debate systems do not reliably outperform those alternatives in their current form. However, tuning hyperparameters improves several systems, including Multi-Persona. This suggests that debate may be especially sensitive to configuration and difficult to optimize, rather than intrinsically less effective than other prompting strategies.

Building on that observation, the paper investigates changes such as adjusting how much agents agree. Such adjustments can significantly improve performance and can exceed all non-debate protocols included in the evaluation. The authors also release implementations and evaluation scripts. The practical finding is conditional: debate can perform strongly with suitable settings, but simply adding a debate protocol does not reliably produce an accuracy advantage.
icml-2024-should-we-be-going-mad-a-look-.tldr: Multi-agent debate does not reliably beat other prompting strategies as configured, but tuning—including agent agreement—can make it outperform evaluated alternatives.

paragraphs: SLEB addresses the deployment cost of large language models by pruning entire transformer blocks. The paper starts from a practical distinction: reducing a model’s size or complexity does not automatically yield a substantial improvement in end-to-end inference speed. Its design therefore focuses on a pruning unit that can directly simplify the model’s sequence of computations.

The motivation is redundancy at the block level. Neighboring transformer blocks can produce highly similar outputs, suggesting that some blocks contribute overlapping processing. SLEB identifies and eliminates redundant blocks, making this coarse structural unit the basis of compression. The approach connects an observation about internal representations to the choice of what should be removed.

Experiments show stronger inference acceleration than previous language-model pruning methods while also retaining better perplexity and accuracy in the reported comparisons. These results support block removal as a promising efficiency strategy. The contribution is the combination of measured processing-speed improvements and favorable model-quality results, addressing the practical goal of making inference faster while preserving useful language-model behavior.
icml-2024-sleb-streamlining-llms-through.tldr: SLEB removes redundant transformer blocks, reporting better inference acceleration, perplexity, and accuracy than previous pruning methods.

paragraphs: SPADE uses sparsity to improve explanations of an already trained neural network. Existing approaches may require sparse training or alter the network’s general behavior by pruning afterward. This paper instead makes sparsity a preprocessing step within the interpretation procedure, tailored to the particular sample being explained.

Given a model and a target input, SPADE prunes connections to retain those most important for that sample. The resulting reduced network acts as a trace of the computation used for the input, and an interpretation method is then applied to that trace. The approach imposes no constraints on how the original model was trained and preserves its inference behavior on the target sample.

The authors report significantly more accurate image saliency maps across several interpretation methods after SPADE preprocessing. They also find that neuron visualizations become more useful for people reasoning about network behavior. The contribution is a way to simplify the object being interpreted while retaining the relevant sample behavior, allowing sparsity to support explanation without requiring a generally sparse deployed model.
icml-2024-spade-sparsity-guided-debuggin.tldr: SPADE applies sample-specific pruning during interpretation to improve saliency maps and neuron visualizations while preserving the model’s behavior on the target sample.

paragraphs: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapts pretrained models at lower cost, but its effectiveness calls for a theoretical explanation. This paper uses a PAC-Bayesian generalization bound to study that question. It interprets pretraining as a change in the prior distribution that yields a tighter bound on generalization error.

The authors examine this interpretation through two properties of the pretrained model: oscillations in the loss landscape and quasi-sparsity in the gradient distribution. Together, these analyses connect the proposed explanation of pretraining to the behavior of optimization during adaptation. The sparse structure observed in gradients motivates focusing fine-tuning changes on selected parameters.

Based on this reasoning, the paper introduces Sparse Increment Fine-Tuning, or SIFT, a gradient-based sparse fine-tuning algorithm. Evaluations on tasks including the GLUE benchmark and instruction tuning support its effectiveness. The work links a generalization-bound perspective to a concrete adaptation method: the theory motivates sparse updates, and the task evaluations assess whether that strategy works in practice. The abstract does not claim that one sparse update pattern suffices for every task.
icml-2024-sparse-is-enough-in-fine-tunin.tldr: The paper motivates sparse fine-tuning through a PAC-Bayesian view of pretraining and introduces SIFT, validated on GLUE and instruction-tuning tasks.

paragraphs: Implicit-depth neural networks describe their computation through a fixed point rather than only through a prescribed stack of layers. A central question is whether such a point exists and whether it is unique. Without those guarantees, the model’s definition can leave room for issues involving stability, performance, and reproducibility.

This paper develops an analysis based on subhomogeneous operators and nonlinear Perron-Frobenius theory. These mathematical tools provide a framework for establishing existence and uniqueness of fixed points. Compared with related earlier analyses, the framework allows weaker assumptions on the parameter matrices, giving designers more flexibility while retaining conditions under which the implicit network is well-defined.

The authors illustrate the resulting subhomogeneous networks with feedforward, convolutional, and graph neural network examples. These examples demonstrate the framework’s application across different network forms. The main contribution is therefore a broader mathematical basis for constructing well-defined implicit models, accompanied by performance illustrations. The guarantees come through the proposed analytical framework; the abstract does not claim that every unconstrained implicit network has a unique solution.
icml-2024-subhomogeneous-deep-equilibriu.tldr: Subhomogeneous operator theory establishes fixed-point existence and uniqueness for implicit networks under weaker parameter-matrix assumptions than related analyses.

paragraphs: SurfPro generates protein sequences from a desired surface and its biochemical properties. Its motivation is that protein function depends on both geometric shape and chemical characteristics. Supplying both kinds of information gives the model a description of the functional surface it should use to guide sequence generation.

The architecture contains a hierarchical encoder that progressively represents the surface’s geometry and biochemical features. An autoregressive decoder then produces the amino acid sequence. This connects a continuous surface description to a discrete sequence, using the encoded surface information as the basis for designing a protein.

The authors evaluate SurfPro on the CATH 4.2 inverse-folding benchmark and on protein-binder and enzyme-design tasks. It consistently exceeds previous state-of-the-art inverse-folding methods in the reported evaluations, reaching 57.78% sequence recovery on CATH 4.2. It also achieves higher success rates measured through protein–protein binding and enzyme–substrate interaction scores. These findings support surface-conditioned generation across the evaluated tasks, with the functional-design results specifically expressed through those interaction-based scores.
icml-2024-surfpro-functional-protein-des.tldr: SurfPro generates protein sequences from surface geometry and biochemical features, improving sequence recovery and interaction-based design scores in its evaluations.

paragraphs: Least-privilege learning aims to create representations that are useful for an intended prediction task while preventing inference of sensitive information outside that task. The appeal is to expose only what the task needs. This paper turns that previously informal aspiration into a formal principle and investigates whether it can be achieved.

The authors prove a fundamental trade-off between task utility and information leakage beyond the intended task. Under their formalization, a representation cannot simultaneously provide high utility and prevent inference of every attribute other than the task label. The result concerns the achievable combination of these goals, regardless of which technique learns the feature mapping.

Experiments across many learning techniques, model architectures, and datasets support the theoretical result. Its significance is that changing the representation-learning method alone cannot eliminate the stated trade-off. The impossibility concerns the strong goal of blocking all inference beyond the label while preserving high utility; it should not be read as a claim that efforts to reduce particular kinds of leakage are inherently useless.
icml-2024-the-fundamental-limits-of-leas.tldr: The paper formalizes least-privilege learning and proves that high task utility cannot coexist with preventing inference of every attribute beyond the task label.

paragraphs: This paper studies how learned data representations interact with the vectors used by a classifier to distinguish classes. It introduces two matrix-information measures: the mutual information ratio, MIR, and the entropy difference ratio, HDR. Inspired by Neural Collapse, the authors derive theoretical optimal values for both measures when that phenomenon occurs.

Experiments use these measures to interpret standard training dynamics, linear mode connectivity, and the effects of label smoothing and pruning. The authors also examine grokking, where generalization emerges long after a model has fitted its training data. MIR and HDR provide a common analytical perspective on changes in the relationship between representations and classification heads across these phenomena.

The paper then moves from measurement to intervention by adding MIR and HDR as loss terms in supervised and semi-supervised learning. These terms are intended to improve information interactions among samples and class heads. Empirical results support their effectiveness, suggesting that the same quantities can help explain training behavior and provide objectives that improve the training procedure.
icml-2024-unveiling-the-dynamics-of-info.tldr: MIR and HDR quantify interactions between representations and classifier heads, helping explain training phenomena and empirically improving training when used as loss terms.
